trends.title: Software-defined vehicles are pulling engineering work into India
trends.summary: Global suppliers keep adding Indian engineering capacity for software-defined mobility, cybersecurity and virtual validation. Bengaluru and Pune are where most of it is happening.

items.title: thyssenkrupp Automotive Technology opens Pune engineering centre, plans 300-plus workforce
items.summary: The new capability centre already has more than 120 engineers on software-defined mobility, cybersecurity and advanced chassis work, and plans to pass 300.
items.script:
thyssenkrupp Automotive Technology has opened a new engineering centre in Pune. The company calls it a global capability centre. It already employs more than one hundred and twenty engineers, and the plan is to grow beyond three hundred. The work there covers three areas: software-defined mobility, cybersecurity, and advanced chassis systems.

Let's unpack why those three areas sit together. thyssenkrupp is best known in automotive for steering systems and dampers, the mechanical heart of the chassis. But a modern steering system is no longer just a column, a rack and a hydraulic pump. Electric power steering uses a motor, a torque sensor and an electronic control unit that decides how much assistance to give at every moment. The next step is steer-by-wire, where there is no mechanical link between the steering wheel and the road wheels at all. The driver's input becomes a stream of data, and actuators at the front axle turn the wheels.

Once steering becomes software and data, two things follow. First, the function can be updated and improved over the life of the vehicle, which is the core idea of the software-defined vehicle. Second, it becomes a target. If an attacker could inject false messages onto the network that carries steering commands, the consequences would be severe. That is why cybersecurity engineers now sit next to chassis engineers. Standards such as I S O twenty one four three four and the U N regulation R one five five require carmakers and suppliers to analyse threats, protect communication with techniques like secure onboard communication, and monitor vehicles in the field.

Chassis functions are also safety critical, so the same software must satisfy functional safety under I S O twenty six two six two. Steer-by-wire typically needs redundant sensors, redundant power supplies and fail-operational designs, meaning the system must keep working safely even after a fault.

Why Pune? India has become one of the largest pools of automotive software and validation talent in the world. Many European and American suppliers now run their embedded software, model-based development, simulation and testing from Indian centres, often working around the clock with teams in Europe.

For engineers and students, the message is clear. Skills that combine embedded software, vehicle networks, functional safety and cybersecurity are in demand, and the jobs are increasingly being created here in India. If you are studying chassis control, it is worth learning how those systems communicate and how they are protected, not just how they are tuned.

You can read the full report on E T Auto using the link on this page.

items.title: SDVs, AI and virtual engineering emerge as key drivers of India's automotive engineering shift
items.summary: Industry speakers describe vehicles that are updated over the air and validated virtually, and what that changes in engineering teams.
items.script:
Software-defined vehicles, artificial intelligence and virtual engineering are emerging as the main forces reshaping automotive engineering in India. Industry leaders described how carmakers and technology companies are preparing for vehicles that are updated continuously, validated virtually and adapted over their lifetime.

Let's start with the software-defined vehicle, or S D V. In a traditional car, each function lives in its own electronic control unit with its own fixed software. Adding a feature often means adding another box. In a software-defined vehicle, the electrical and electronic architecture is reorganised around a few powerful central computers and zone controllers. Functions become software applications that can be added or improved through over-the-air updates, long after the car leaves the factory. Middleware such as adaptive AUTOSAR and service-oriented communication like SOME over I P make this possible.

This has a big consequence for testing. If software keeps changing, you cannot rely only on physical prototypes and test drives to validate each release. That is where virtual engineering comes in. Engineers build digital models of the vehicle, its sensors and its environment, and run software against them. You may have heard the terms model in the loop, software in the loop and hardware in the loop. Together they let teams test thousands of scenarios automatically, including dangerous ones that would be impossible to try on a real road. Digital twins extend this idea by keeping a virtual copy of a real vehicle or system that is updated with field data.

Artificial intelligence plays several roles. It powers perception in driver assistance systems, it helps generate and prioritise test cases, it can assist engineers in writing and reviewing code, and it can analyse data coming back from vehicles in the field.

Why does this matter for India in particular? Indian engineering centres already carry out a large share of the world's automotive software development and validation. As the industry moves toward continuous software delivery and virtual testing, the skills in demand shift toward cloud tooling, continuous integration pipelines, simulation, and of course the safety and cybersecurity processes that keep updates trustworthy.

For students, a practical takeaway: learn how the V-model maps onto continuous integration, get comfortable with simulation tools, and understand how over-the-air updates are secured. Those are the building blocks of the software-defined vehicle.

You can read the full feature on E T Auto through the link on this page.

items.title: AutoEV Bharat 2026, Bengaluru: A Must-Visit Show for Automotive OEMs
items.summary: A Bengaluru exhibition covering automotive semiconductors, sensors, batteries and smart manufacturing for OEMs.
items.script:
AutoEV Bharat 2026, the fifth edition of the show, will take place from the ninth to the eleventh of December at the K T P O exhibition centre in Whitefield, Bengaluru. Alongside it, the AutoEV Tech Vision Summit will run on the tenth and eleventh of December at the same venue. The event is aimed at carmakers, E V manufacturers, tier suppliers, engineers and technology leaders.

The list of themes reads like a map of where vehicle technology is heading. On the vehicle side, the show covers advanced driver assistance systems, automotive A I, software-defined vehicles, automotive semiconductors, embedded systems and connected vehicles. On electrification, it covers battery technology and battery management systems, charging infrastructure, electric motors, power electronics and energy storage. And it also includes testing and validation, simulation, digital twins, cybersecurity, robotics and smart manufacturing. The summit sessions focus on software-defined vehicles, functional safety, cybersecurity, A I in automotive engineering, advanced batteries, charging and digital manufacturing.

Notice how much of this is electronics and software. A battery pack, for example, is not just cells. It needs a battery management system that measures every cell's voltage and temperature, estimates the state of charge and the state of health, balances the cells and protects them from over-charge, over-discharge and thermal runaway. The traction inverter uses power semiconductors, increasingly silicon carbide, switching hundreds of amps thousands of times a second, controlled by field-oriented control algorithms. Each of these subsystems is a topic in its own right.

Functional safety and cybersecurity appearing together on the summit agenda is also telling. As more functions move into software and vehicles become connected, both I S O twenty six two six two for safety and I S O twenty one four three four for security have become everyday engineering requirements, not specialist topics.

Why go to a show like this? For students, exhibitions are one of the best ways to see real hardware up close: battery modules, inverters, E C U boards, test benches and hardware-in-the-loop rigs. You can talk to the engineers who built them, ask how they are tested, and learn which skills companies are hiring for. For working engineers, it is a quick way to scan suppliers and tools in one place.

Bengaluru is a fitting location, as the city hosts many of the engineering centres working on these technologies.

The full preview from E L E Times is linked on this page.

items.title: Auto manufacturing needs greater R&D investment to tap next growth phase: CII chairman
items.summary: CII argues that electronics, software and AI are converging with mechanical engineering, so Indian suppliers need to spend more on R&D.
items.script:
The chairman of the Confederation of Indian Industry has called for much greater investment in research and development by India's automotive manufacturers. The argument is that the next phase of growth will depend on technology, as electronics, software, artificial intelligence, advanced materials and mechanical engineering converge and change both the products and the way they are made.

Why is this convergence such a big deal? For most of the last century, a car's value was mainly mechanical: the engine, the transmission, the body and the suspension. Indian manufacturing grew strong by building these parts at scale and at low cost. Today, a growing share of a vehicle's cost and value sits in electronics and software. A modern car can carry dozens of electronic control units, several kilometres of wiring, cameras, radar sensors and a central computer running millions of lines of code. In an electric vehicle, the battery, the motor controller and the power electronics can make up a large part of the bill of materials.

This shift changes what it means to be a competitive supplier. Building a part to a drawing is no longer enough. Carmakers increasingly want suppliers who can design the system, write the software, validate it and keep updating it. That requires engineering teams, test labs, simulation tools and long development cycles, all of which need sustained research spending.

The manufacturing side is changing too. Factories use more sensors, data and A I to predict machine failures, check quality with cameras and plan production. So the same digital skills are needed on the shop floor as in the vehicle.

India has an advantage in software talent, and global companies already run large engineering centres here. A point often made by industry observers is that much of that work is done for foreign companies, and that many Indian component makers invest less of their revenue in their own research than their global peers. Building intellectual property, rather than only providing engineering services, is seen as the way to capture more value.

Government programmes such as the production linked incentive scheme for automobiles and auto components, and the semiconductor mission, are meant to support this. But the message from industry bodies is that private investment must rise as well.

For students and young engineers, this is encouraging. It suggests that demand will keep growing for people who understand electronics, embedded software, power electronics and data, and who can connect them with mechanical design.

The full article from E T Manufacturing is linked on this page.

trends.title: Power electronics and electrified powertrains
trends.summary: Better high-voltage DC/DC conversion, hybrids built for several powertrain options, and Formula E as a test bed for inverter and motor technology.

items.title: Flex Wins 2026 Automotive News PACE Award for Fully Symmetric HV DC/DC Architecture
items.summary: The award-winning DC/DC design aims to simplify the vehicle's electrical architecture and reduce dependence on the auxiliary low-voltage network.
items.script:
Flex has won a 2026 Automotive News PACE Award for its high voltage D C to D C converter for electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles. The PACE Awards are judged by an independent panel and recognise supplier innovations with real technical and business impact. Flex says this is its third PACE Award in two years. An earlier one recognised a backup D C to D C converter that keeps essential drive-by-wire systems powered.

First, what does a D C to D C converter do in an electric car? The traction battery runs at around four hundred or eight hundred volts. But lights, infotainment, control units, pumps and fans still run from a low voltage network, usually twelve volts. The D C to D C converter steps the high voltage down to supply that network, and it replaces the alternator you would find in a petrol car.

Flex describes its design as fully symmetric, based on a dual active bridge topology. Here is the idea. You have two full bridges of power transistors, one on each side of a high-frequency transformer. Each bridge switches at high frequency, and the power flow is controlled by the phase shift between them. Because the two sides are built the same way, power can flow in either direction. The transformer also provides galvanic isolation, which is essential for safety, so the high voltage side is electrically separated from the low voltage side the occupants can touch.

Flex says the converter accepts a wide input voltage range, works with both four hundred and eight hundred volt batteries, supports bidirectional energy flow and responds quickly to changing loads. It can also be integrated with onboard chargers, inverters and software-based power management.

Why does bidirectional flow matter? It means the low voltage side can be supported directly from the high voltage battery, and in some cases energy can flow back the other way. Flex claims this reduces reliance on the auxiliary twelve volt battery, simplifies the electrical architecture, saves weight and cost and improves reliability. As vehicles adopt by-wire steering and braking, keeping the low voltage supply stable becomes a safety issue, not just a convenience.

For students of power electronics, the dual active bridge is a great example of how topology choice drives system benefits. Look up soft switching, phase-shift control and isolation requirements to go deeper.

The full press release from Flex is linked on this page.

items.title: Mahindra Racing strengthens GEN4 technical programme with Valeo as Official Performance and Engineering Partner
items.summary: Valeo brings its electrification know-how to Mahindra's Formula E GEN4 programme.
items.script:
Mahindra Racing has named Valeo as its official performance and engineering partner for the Formula E GEN4 era. The partnership builds on an existing relationship: Valeo already supplies electric axles for Mahindra's road vehicles. For racing, the work focuses on two areas: software for motor control, and hardware testing of the powertrain components. Mahindra's GEN4 car is called the M13 Electro. Valeo's work will be led mainly from its research labs and advanced technology centre in Erlangen, Germany.

Let's look at what motor control software actually does. A racing electric motor is typically a permanent magnet synchronous machine, driven by an inverter that converts the battery's direct current into three-phase alternating current. The control algorithm, usually field-oriented control, measures the rotor position and the phase currents thousands of times per second. It then decides exactly how to switch the inverter's transistors so the magnetic field in the stator stays at the right angle to the rotor. Get it right and you get maximum torque for every amp. Get it slightly wrong and you waste energy as heat.

In Formula E, energy is strictly limited, so efficiency decides races. Valeo is developing custom control algorithms to manage the motor precisely, optimise energy use and reduce losses over a race distance. Small gains in efficiency translate directly into more usable energy in the final laps, or the ability to push harder when it matters.

The second part is test benches. Valeo will provide high precision benches to fine-tune and stress-test the powertrain's core electronics. A test bench lets engineers run the motor and inverter through repeatable load cycles, measure efficiency maps, check thermal behaviour and find weaknesses before they appear on track.

Mahindra describes this as a race to road approach. The same disciplines, precise control, minimal losses and rigorous testing, apply directly to production electric cars, where efficiency means more range from the same battery.

For students, this story is a good reminder that an E V powertrain is as much about software and power electronics as it is about the motor itself. If you want to go deeper, study field-oriented control, space vector modulation, and how inverter losses are split between conduction and switching.

The full press release from Mahindra is linked on this page.

items.title: Toyota Develops New Hybrid for Future Multi-Pathway Vehicle Platforms
items.summary: Toyota's next hybrid system is designed for platforms that keep several powertrain options open at once.
items.script:
Toyota has described a new hybrid system for its future multi-pathway vehicle platforms. It is built around a new family of one point five litre, four-cylinder engines, in naturally aspirated and turbocharged versions. The engine, electric motors, power control units and inverters are developed together as a single compact package, designed to reduce both electrical and mechanical losses. Toyota is targeting more than fifteen percent better fuel economy, through lower friction, better thermal management, lower electrical losses and less aerodynamic drag.

The phrase multi-pathway is central to Toyota's strategy. Instead of betting only on battery electric vehicles, Toyota is designing a common architecture that can carry battery electric, plug-in hybrid and conventional hybrid powertrains. Because the new engine and hybrid unit are compact, they allow lower bonnet lines, so the same body can accept different powertrains. That lets factories change the production mix as demand shifts and spreads development costs across larger volumes.

Why does integrating the motor, inverter and engine matter? In a hybrid, energy is constantly converted: chemical energy in fuel becomes mechanical work, which can become electrical energy in the generator, which is stored in the battery and then converted back to motion by the motor. Every conversion loses a little energy, in the inverter's switching transistors, in the motor windings and in the wiring between components. Placing them close together shortens cables, reduces losses and saves weight. Shared cooling circuits also help with thermal management, which is critical for both power electronics and the engine.

Toyota's hybrids typically use a power split device, a planetary gearset that blends engine and motor power without a conventional gearbox. The power control unit, with its inverter and boost converter, decides moment by moment how power flows. Much of the efficiency gain in a new generation comes from improving these electronics and the control strategy, not just the engine.

Toyota also says the system is being developed to run on renewable and carbon-neutral fuels, and that it plans to sell the new engine and hybrid technology to other companies. It reports more than thirty five million electrified vehicles sold to date.

For students, this is a good case study in system-level optimisation, where the biggest gains come from how components work together.

The full article from Electronic Design is linked on this page.

items.title: Growth of the Automotive Power Electronics Market Driven by EVs
items.summary: A market report linking growth in automotive power electronics to EV adoption. It is promotional, so read the figures with caution.
items.script:
A new market report says the automotive power electronics sector is growing quickly as it adapts to the rapid rise of electric vehicles and advanced vehicle systems. Reports like this are published by market research firms to promote their full studies, so their forecasts should be read with some caution. But the underlying trend is real, and worth understanding.

So what counts as power electronics in a vehicle? It is the hardware that converts and controls electrical energy. In an electric car, the main pieces are the traction inverter, which turns the battery's direct current into alternating current to drive the motor; the onboard charger, which converts alternating current from the grid into direct current for the battery; and the D C to D C converter, which steps the high voltage down to supply the twelve volt network. Even in petrol cars, power electronics drive electric power steering, fuel pumps, cooling fans and L E D lighting.

At the heart of all of these are power semiconductor switches. For decades, the workhorses were silicon M O S F E Ts and I G B Ts. Now, wide bandgap materials are taking over in high-voltage applications. Silicon carbide transistors can block higher voltages, switch faster and run hotter with lower losses. That is why many eight hundred volt electric cars use silicon carbide in their inverters. Gallium nitride is gaining ground in lower-power converters and onboard chargers, where very fast switching allows smaller magnetic components.

Why do these choices matter? Every percent of efficiency in the inverter becomes extra driving range, or a smaller battery for the same range. Lower losses also mean less heat, so cooling systems can be smaller and lighter. Faster switching shrinks inductors and capacitors, reducing the size and cost of the whole unit.

The challenges are also real. Fast switching creates electromagnetic interference that must be filtered. High temperatures stress solder joints and packages, so reliability engineering is a big part of the job. And control software, from pulse width modulation to protection logic, has to be fast and functionally safe.

For students, power electronics is one of the most valuable skill sets in the E V era. Start with buck and boost converters, then study inverters, gate drivers and thermal design.

The market report is linked on this page; treat its numbers as indicative.

trends.title: ECUs, cameras and the electronics supply chain
trends.summary: Camera modules, engine control modules and cockpit electronics are changing hands. Capital needs are pushing smaller players out.

items.title: Foxconn acquires automotive camera module business from Sony Semiconductor Solutions
items.summary: Foxconn (Hon Hai) is buying Sony's automotive camera module business to grow in ADAS sensing. The initial deal is valued at about ¥7.2 billion (~$45 million).
items.script:
Foxconn, the Taiwanese electronics manufacturer also known as Hon Hai, has agreed to acquire the automotive camera module business of Sony Semiconductor Solutions. The deal includes the business's technology, its customer base, and its experience of supplying carmakers directly. Closing is expected by the end of April 2027, subject to regulatory approval. Reports put the initial transaction at about seven point two billion yen, roughly forty five million U S dollars. Sony's relevant overseas entities will provide transitional support after closing, with the focus on keeping customer service and operations stable.

Why would Foxconn want this? Foxconn already builds huge numbers of camera modules for smartphones and other consumer electronics. Cars are a growing market for cameras. A modern vehicle may carry several of them: a forward camera behind the windscreen for lane keeping and automatic emergency braking, surround-view cameras for parking, rear cameras, and increasingly an interior camera that monitors whether the driver is paying attention. Advanced driver assistance systems depend on these sensors, and demand grows with every new safety regulation.

An automotive camera module is more than a lens and an image sensor. It includes the sensor chip, optics, a circuit board with a serialiser that sends high-speed video over a coaxial cable, and a sealed housing that must survive heat, cold, vibration and water for many years. Automotive image sensors also need high dynamic range, so they can see clearly when driving out of a dark tunnel into bright sunlight, and they must handle flickering L E D traffic lights. Quality requirements are strict, with automotive qualification standards and functional safety considerations.

It is worth noting what Sony is not selling. Sony remains a leading maker of automotive image sensors, the chips inside the camera. This deal concerns the module business, which assembles those sensors into complete camera units. Foxconn's strength in high-volume precision assembly fits that layer of the supply chain.

The deal also fits Foxconn's broader push into vehicles, including its electric vehicle platform efforts. Owning more of the electronics supply chain lets it offer carmakers more complete systems.

For engineers, this is a reminder that sensing hardware is a strategic part of the vehicle, and that consolidation among suppliers is changing who builds what.

The full report is linked on this page.

items.title: BorgWarner Secures Engine Control Module Business With Major Global OEM
items.summary: BorgWarner PowerDrive Systems has won an engine control module programme with a large global OEM. Combustion and hybrid ECUs are still a live business.
items.script:
BorgWarner has won a high-volume contract to supply engine control modules for an internal combustion pick-up truck platform from a long-standing global carmaker. BorgWarner has supplied engine control modules to this customer since 2020, and the new deal extends the relationship to 2034, with production expected to start in 2029.

The engine control module, often called the E C M or engine E C U, is the brain of a combustion engine. It reads sensors such as crankshaft and camshaft position, manifold pressure, air mass flow, coolant temperature and the oxygen sensors in the exhaust. From these, it calculates exactly how much fuel to inject, when to inject it, when to fire the spark plugs and how to control the throttle, turbocharger and exhaust gas recirculation. It does this for every cylinder, every cycle, while keeping emissions within legal limits.

According to the report, this E C M was designed specifically for the platform, with more functions, more flexible control, and a compact layout. It can control diesel, gasoline direct injection and port fuel injection engines, and works with all injectors currently on the market. It uses BorgWarner's own application-specific integrated circuits, an advanced microprocessor, and integrated control of exhaust aftertreatment. Its direct injection control supports fuel pressures of five hundred bar.

Why does five hundred bar matter? In gasoline direct injection, fuel is sprayed straight into the cylinder. Higher pressure produces finer droplets, which mix better with air and burn more completely, reducing particulate emissions. But driving injectors at those pressures needs high-voltage, precisely timed current pulses. That is why custom chips are used: they handle the injector drive stages that a general-purpose microcontroller cannot.

Aftertreatment control is the other big task. Catalytic converters, particulate filters and, on diesels, selective catalytic reduction systems all need precise management, and emissions rules keep tightening.

There is a wider lesson here. While electric vehicles get the headlines, combustion and hybrid powertrains will remain in production for many years, especially in pick-up trucks and commercial vehicles. Engine management remains a busy field for embedded engineers.

BorgWarner's portfolio also includes battery management, motor, transmission and commercial vehicle engine controllers, showing how suppliers are spreading across both combustion and electric technologies.

The full report from Motor India is linked on this page.

items.title: Large capital needs, technology shift behind Pricol Autotech exit, says Vikram Mohan
items.summary: Pricol's promoter family is selling its entire stake, saying the automotive electronics business now needs more capital to stay competitive.
items.script:
The promoter family of Pricol, an Indian automotive component maker, is selling its entire holding in Pricol Autotech, the company's automotive electronics business, which is being demerged into a separate listed company. The buyer is the private equity firm Warburg Pincus. According to the report, Warburg would acquire about thirty eight and a half percent of the demerged company's equity, in a deal worth up to one thousand six hundred and sixty three crore rupees. Chairman Vikram Mohan said the family could not fund the heavy, continuing investment the business needs in technology, manufacturing and talent while keeping majority ownership. He will step down as chairman and managing director of Autotech once the transfer completes, and the current senior team will stay.

This is a useful lens on the economics of automotive electronics. Pricol is known for instrument clusters and other electronic products. Twenty years ago, an instrument cluster was a set of analogue gauges with a few warning lamps. Today it is often a high-resolution digital display, driven by a graphics processor, running a real-time operating system, connected to the vehicle network, and sometimes merged with the infotainment screen into a single cockpit domain controller.

Each step of that evolution raises the cost of staying competitive. You need software teams, displays and graphics expertise, cybersecurity processes, functional safety certification, and the ability to deliver over-the-air updates. Product cycles are shorter, and customers expect suppliers to co-develop features. All of that requires sustained investment, often ahead of revenue.

Mohan said a buyer with deeper finances, stronger management expertise and global reach was better placed to take the business forward. That pattern is visible across the industry. Electronics businesses tend to consolidate, because scale spreads the large fixed costs of software and validation.

Meanwhile, Pricol's remaining businesses are expanding with internal funds and borrowing. These include new plants in Sanand and Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, recently commissioned plants in Mysuru and Narsapura, a large plant in Hosur, and a polymer engineering centre in Coimbatore.

For students and engineers, the takeaway is that automotive electronics is a capital-intensive, fast-moving field. The value increasingly lies in software and system integration, and that is where investment, and hiring, are concentrating.

The full report is linked on this page.

items.title: Marelli secures two honours at 2026 PACE Awards
items.summary: Marelli won recognition for next-generation display technology and vehicle connectivity.
items.script:
Marelli has received two honours at the 2026 Automotive News PACE Awards, both in automotive electronics, covering next-generation display technology and vehicle connectivity. The PACE Awards recognise supplier innovations judged to have real technical and business impact.

Let's look at why displays and connectivity are such active areas. Not long ago, a car's dashboard had analogue dials, and the radio had a small segment display. Today, many vehicles have a digital instrument cluster, a large central touchscreen, sometimes a passenger display, and a head-up display projected onto the windscreen. These screens are becoming larger, curved, and in some cases stretch across the whole dashboard.

That creates engineering challenges well beyond the screen itself. Automotive displays must stay readable in direct sunlight and at night, survive temperatures from well below freezing to the heat of a parked car in summer, and meet strict reliability targets for many years. They must avoid distracting reflections in the windscreen. Technologies such as local dimming, mini L E D backlights and O L E D panels are used to improve contrast and reduce power. Behind the screen, a cockpit domain controller often runs several displays at once from a single high-performance chip, using a hypervisor to keep safety-relevant content, such as warning lamps, separate from infotainment apps.

Connectivity is the other half. A connected car has a telematics control unit with a cellular modem, and increasingly support for five G and vehicle-to-everything communication. Connectivity enables navigation and streaming, but more importantly, it enables over-the-air software updates, remote diagnostics, emergency calls and fleet services. It is also a major attack surface, which is why connectivity units must meet cybersecurity requirements such as U N regulation R one five five.

Displays and connectivity also meet in the software-defined vehicle. When features can be added through software, the screen is where the driver sees them and the connectivity unit is how they arrive.

Marelli is a major global supplier of lighting, electronics and powertrain components. Recognition in these categories reflects how central cockpit electronics and connectivity have become to the value of a vehicle.

For students, cockpit electronics is a field that blends graphics, embedded software, networking and human factors. It is a great area to explore if you enjoy both hardware and user experience.

The full report from Manufacturing Today India is linked on this page.

items.title: FORVIA receives three 2026 Automotive News PACE pilot recognitions
items.summary: FORVIA was recognised for work on high-performance lighting and automotive electronics.
items.script:
FORVIA has received three pilot recognitions at the 2026 Automotive News PACE Awards. The recognitions relate to the company's work on high-performance lighting and automotive electronics technologies. FORVIA is one of the world's largest automotive suppliers, and it includes the lighting and electronics specialist formerly known as Hella.

Lighting is a surprisingly good example of how far electronics has spread into the car. A headlamp used to be a bulb and a reflector. Today, L E D headlamps are controlled by dedicated driver electronics, and many vehicles use adaptive driving beam systems. These use a camera to detect oncoming cars and vehicles ahead, then switch off or dim only the segments of the light beam that would dazzle other drivers, while keeping the rest of the road brightly lit. High-definition systems go further, with thousands or even more than a million individually controllable pixels, able to project guidance lines or warnings onto the road.

All of this requires fast communication between the camera, a control unit and the lamp, precise current control for the L E Ds, and careful thermal management, because L E D efficiency and lifetime fall as temperatures rise. Lighting functions are also safety relevant. If a headlamp controller fails, the system must fall back to a safe state, so functional safety principles apply.

Lighting is also becoming a communication channel. Exterior light signatures, welcome animations and signals for automated driving modes are all being explored, and interior ambient lighting can warn the driver or show charging status.

The Automotive News PACE pilot recognitions are given to innovations that are being tested or piloted with customers, before full commercial launch. That makes them a useful early indicator of what may appear in production vehicles in the next few years.

For engineers, the lesson is that every part of the vehicle, even the lamps, now involves sensors, embedded software and networking. Courses in power electronics for L E D drivers, image processing for camera-based lighting, and functional safety are all relevant here.

The press release from FORVIA is linked on this page.

items.title: Japan Eyes Sri Lanka For Automotive Electronics Manufacturing
items.summary: Japanese firms are looking at Sri Lanka as a production base, citing Lanka Harness's export record and spare capacity.
items.script:
Japan is considering Sri Lanka as a manufacturing base for automotive electronics, as part of a proposed Japan, India and Sri Lanka economic corridor, supported by Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry and the trade agency JETRO. Japan's ambassador to Sri Lanka, Akio Isomata, recently visited the company Lanka Harness and praised its precision manufacturing and quality.

Lanka Harness makes automotive wire harnesses and safety components, including impact sensors used for airbags and seatbelts. It supplies major global carmakers and exports to seventeen countries, including Japan, India, China and Romania. It reports annual revenue of more than eighty million U S dollars and supports about a thousand direct and indirect jobs. The company started in 2002 with an initial Japanese investment of eight million dollars, and it reports a defect rate of one part per million. It has completed a new factory with spare capacity for Japanese customers, including those looking at operations in India. Under the India Sri Lanka free trade agreement, products with at least thirty five percent local value addition get preferential access to the Indian market.

The wire harness deserves more attention than it usually gets. It is the vehicle's nervous system: thousands of wires, connectors and terminals that carry power and signals between every sensor, actuator and control unit. A modern car's harness can weigh tens of kilograms and run to several kilometres of cable. It is still largely assembled by hand, which is why harness production tends to locate in countries with skilled, cost-competitive labour.

Harness design is changing fast. Zonal electrical architectures aim to shorten and simplify harnesses by placing zone controllers around the car, each serving nearby devices. Automotive Ethernet is replacing some point-to-point wiring for high-bandwidth data. And forty eight volt systems allow thinner cables for the same power.

Airbag impact sensors show the safety side. These sensors detect a crash within milliseconds and send the signal that fires the airbags and pretensions the seatbelts. Reliability is non-negotiable, which explains the emphasis on parts-per-million quality.

For engineers, this story highlights that the supply chain for automotive electronics is regional and strategic. Countries are competing to host it, and quality and trade rules shape where it goes.

The full article from Electronics For You is linked on this page.

trends.title: Shared platforms and standardisation
trends.summary: To cut cost and development time, carmakers are sharing platforms and agreeing on common parts.

items.title: Toyota, Nissan, Honda back Japan plan to standardize parts, lower costs
items.summary: Japan's carmakers association (JAMA) proposes industry-wide parts standards. No timeline has been given yet.
items.script:
Japan's carmakers, including Toyota, Nissan and Honda, are backing an industry plan to standardise vehicle parts in order to lower costs. The plan comes from the Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association, known as JAMA. According to the report, no concrete timeline has been set yet for implementing the standardisation goals.

Why would fierce competitors agree to share parts? The answer lies in rising costs. Each new generation of vehicles adds more electronics, more software, and more development work for safety, emissions and cybersecurity regulations. At the same time, Japanese carmakers face strong price competition, especially from Chinese manufacturers who have moved quickly in electric vehicles and in-car software. When every company designs its own version of a part that customers never see, the industry pays for the same engineering many times over.

Standardisation is not new in the automotive world. Connectors, fasteners, diagnostic interfaces such as the O B D port, and communication protocols such as C A N are all standardised, which is why tools and components work across brands. AUTOSAR is another example: carmakers and suppliers agreed on a common software architecture for control units, so that suppliers can reuse software and carmakers can integrate it more easily. Competition then shifts to the features that customers actually notice.

For electronics, standard parts could mean common semiconductors, shared control unit hardware, or common interfaces between components. That would help suppliers achieve larger production volumes, which lowers unit costs and can make supply chains more resilient. The semiconductor shortage of recent years showed how vulnerable the industry is when many slightly different chips are each made in small quantities.

There are trade-offs. Standards take time to agree, and companies worry about losing differentiation. Deciding which parts are truly non-differentiating is often the hardest part of such efforts, which may explain the lack of a timeline.

For engineers, standardisation is a reminder that good interfaces are as important as good components. If you are designing a module, thinking about how it fits into a standard architecture makes it far more valuable.

The full report from Automotive News is linked on this page.

items.title: Tata Group draws Honda and Hyundai interest in vehicle and tech sharing
items.summary: Honda and Hyundai are reported to be exploring platform and technology sharing with Tata.
items.script:
Reports say Honda and Hyundai are exploring opportunities to share vehicles, platforms and technology with the Tata Group. The report describes global manufacturers looking at cooperation with the Indian automotive major, rather than any agreement that has been signed.

Platform and technology sharing has become common across the global industry, and it is worth understanding why. A vehicle platform is the shared engineering foundation underneath a car: the floor structure, suspension layout, powertrain mounting, and increasingly the electrical and electronic architecture. Developing a new platform costs a great deal of money and takes several years. Sharing it across more models and more brands spreads that cost over more vehicles.

Electrification makes sharing even more attractive. Battery electric platforms, battery packs, motors and power electronics require heavy investment, and suppliers offer better prices for larger volumes. Tata Motors has invested significantly in electric vehicles for the Indian market, and Tata Group companies also have strengths in software and engineering services. For a global carmaker, partnering in India can provide access to cost-competitive engineering, local manufacturing and an understanding of the Indian market, which is one of the largest in the world.

Software is a growing part of these discussions. In a software-defined vehicle, the electronic architecture, the operating system and the cloud services are expensive to build and maintain. Several carmakers around the world now share software stacks or collaborate on them, rather than each building everything alone.

There are challenges, of course. Partners must agree on which parts are shared and which remain unique to each brand, protect their intellectual property, and align development schedules. Sharing electronics also means aligning cybersecurity and functional safety processes, so that each partner can certify the vehicle under its own responsibility.

For engineers and students in India, partnerships like these could mean more global programmes developed locally, with Indian teams working on platforms used around the world.

As always with reports of early-stage talks, it is best to treat this as a direction of travel rather than a done deal.

The full report from Team-B H P is linked on this page.

items.title: 2027 Hyundai ELANTRA and 2028 ELANTRA Hybrid Revealed at Los Angeles Auto Show
items.summary: The eighth-generation Elantra adds more connectivity and driver-assistance features.
items.script:
Hyundai has revealed the eighth-generation 2027 Elantra and the 2028 Elantra Hybrid at the Los Angeles Auto Show. Beyond the new design, the electronics upgrades are significant.

Start with the cockpit. Every trim gets a twelve point nine inch full H D touchscreen running Hyundai's Pleos Connect infotainment platform, which is built on Android Automotive. Wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto are supported. Connectivity includes cloud services, a Wi-Fi hotspot and Hyundai's app ecosystem. There is a new voice assistant called Gleo A I, built on a large language model, which can handle several commands at once and recognise whether the driver or a passenger is speaking. Software and feature updates can be delivered over the air, without a visit to the dealer. Hyundai has kept physical buttons and knobs for audio and climate, a choice many drivers appreciate.

Android Automotive is worth explaining. Unlike Android Auto, which projects your phone onto the car's screen, Android Automotive is an operating system that runs directly on the car's own computer. The carmaker customises it and connects it to vehicle functions. It is one of the clearest signs of how consumer software platforms are moving into vehicles.

On safety, the SmartSense suite includes forward collision avoidance that can detect pedestrians, cyclists, and vehicles when turning at junctions or coming the other way. It also has blind-spot and rear cross-traffic warnings, lane keeping with haptic feedback, adaptive cruise control with stop and go, and on top trims, a driver monitoring system that checks whether the driver is paying attention. These features rely on fusing data from cameras and radar sensors.

The hybrid gets a meaningful upgrade. The 2028 Elantra Hybrid combines a one point six litre engine with a six-speed dual clutch transmission, for one hundred and fifty five horsepower combined, up from one hundred and thirty nine. The electric motor grows from thirty two to forty five kilowatts, and the battery from one point three two to one point four nine kilowatt hours. Hyundai targets up to fifty three miles per gallon combined, though that is not yet an official rating. A stay mode can run the climate, audio and lights from the hybrid battery for around twenty to thirty minutes while parked.

For students, this mainstream sedan shows how quickly over-the-air updates, A I assistants and sensor fusion have become standard features.
